analogy.p: Think of speed as how fast water flows from a tap: litres per minute. Compound units always tell you 'how much per one of something'. If the tap flows at 10 litres per minute, then in 5 minutes you get 50 litres, just as at 60 km/h you cover 120 km in 2 hours. Density is like how tightly packed the water balloons are in a box, and pressure is like standing on one foot versus two. The analogy breaks down because a real tap rate can change continuously, whereas the formulae give an average value unless you are told the rate is constant.
analogy.t: Rates are like a tap and a bath

bullets: **Speed** = distance ÷ time (how far per unit of time).
**Density** = mass ÷ volume (how much mass per unit of volume).
**Pressure** = force ÷ area (how much force per unit of area).
Also expected: **rates of pay** (e.g. £ per hour) and **unit pricing** (e.g. pence per gram) to compare value.
Each formula can be rearranged: you must be able to find the missing quantity whichever two you are given.
Units matter: answers need correct compound units such as km/h, g/cm³ or N/m².
The word **per** signals division: 'miles per hour' means miles ÷ hours.
core.p: The Edexcel specification (Ratio, proportion and rates of change) requires you to **use compound units** such as speed, rates of pay, unit pricing, density and pressure. A compound unit is made by combining two different measurements, so it describes a **rate**: how much of one quantity there is per one unit of another. You must be able to use the formulae, convert between different units, rearrange the formulae to find any of the three quantities, and interpret the results in context. The topic appears on both calculator and non-calculator papers, often as multi-step problems.

bullets: S = D ÷ T; D = S × T; T = D ÷ S.
Units: m/s (metres per second), km/h (kilometres per hour), miles per hour (mph).
Time conversion: 30 minutes = 0.5 h; 15 minutes = 0.25 h; 20 minutes = 1/3 h (use the fraction, not 0.33); 2 h 45 min = 2.75 h.
To convert a decimal hour to minutes, multiply by 60: 0.4 h = 24 minutes.
Example: 150 km in 2.5 h gives speed 150 ÷ 2.5 = 60 km/h.
Example: at 48 km/h, a journey of 20 km takes 20 ÷ 48 = 0.41666 h = 25 minutes.
State the answer with the unit and in the form the question asks (e.g. time in hours and minutes).
core.p: **Speed** is the distance travelled per unit of time. The formula is speed = distance ÷ time, which rearranges to distance = speed × time and time = distance ÷ speed. These are often remembered with a formula triangle, with distance on top and speed and time at the bottom. Time must be in a unit that matches the speed unit: if the speed is in km/h the time must be in hours, so minutes have to be converted by dividing by 60.

bullets: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
Example: 150 km in 2.5 h then 90 km in 1.5 h: total distance 240 km, total time 4 h, average speed **60 km/h**.
Adding the speeds and halving (60 and 60 gives 60) only works by luck here - in general it is wrong.
If the question gives the same distance at two speeds, find each time, add, then divide the total distance by the total time.
Return trips: out at 30 km/h and back at 60 km/h over 60 km each way: times 2 h and 1 h, total 120 km in 3 h = **40 km/h**, not 45.
A stop (e.g. a 30-minute break) is included in total time for the average speed of the whole journey.
Check: the average speed must lie between the slowest and fastest speeds.
core.p: **Average speed** is the **total distance** divided by the **total time** for a whole journey. It is not found by averaging two speeds unless the times are equal. A journey with different parts at different speeds must be split: work out the distance or time for each part, add them, then divide. Any stops count towards the total time if the question asks for the average speed for the whole journey including stops.

bullets: Gradient = (change in distance) ÷ (change in time) = speed.
Horizontal section: **stationary** (distance not changing).
Straight sloping section: **constant speed**; curved sections: speed is changing.
Steeper gradient means faster speed.
A line returning to zero distance shows travel back to the start.
To find the speed from a graph, choose two points on the section, work out the rise and run, and divide; give the unit (e.g. km/h).
Average speed for the whole trip uses the total distance travelled (there and back) divided by total time, not the displacement.
core.p: A **distance-time graph** shows how far an object has travelled from the start over time. The **gradient** (steepness) of the line equals the **speed**, because gradient = change in distance ÷ change in time. A horizontal line means the object is stationary; a steeper line means faster travel; a line sloping back down means the object is returning. You should be able to read values, calculate speeds from sections, and describe the journey in words.

bullets: D = M ÷ V; M = D × V; V = M ÷ D.
If mass is in g and volume in cm³, density is in **g/cm³**; if mass is in kg and volume in m³, density is in **kg/m³**.
Example: a 120 cm³ block with mass 1020 g has density 1020 ÷ 120 = 8.5 g/cm³.
Example: 5 cm³ of a metal of density 7.8 g/cm³ has mass 5 × 7.8 = 39 g.
Volume formulae are often needed first: cuboid = length × width × height; cylinder = π r² h.
An object floats in water if its density is less than 1 g/cm³ (less than water).
Density of a mixture or alloy: total mass ÷ total volume, not the average of the densities.
core.p: **Density** is the mass of a substance per unit volume. The formula is density = mass ÷ volume, so mass = density × volume and volume = mass ÷ density. A dense material has a lot of mass packed into a small volume. Common units are g/cm³ and kg/m³, and the unit of density must match the units used for mass and volume. Water has a density of 1 g/cm³ (1000 kg/m³), which is a useful reference value.

bullets: P = F ÷ A; F = P × A; A = F ÷ P.
Units: **N/m² = Pa** if the area is in m²; N/cm² if the area is in cm².
Example: force 600 N on an area of 0.25 m² gives pressure 600 ÷ 0.25 = 2400 N/m².
Example: pressure 4500 N/m² on area 0.02 m² gives force 4500 × 0.02 = 90 N.
**Pressure is inversely proportional to area** for a fixed force: halve the area and the pressure doubles.
Force is often the **weight** of an object; weight (N) = mass (kg) × 10 N/kg is given in the question if needed.
When an object rests on several feet or sides, the area is the total area in contact with the surface.
core.p: **Pressure** is the force acting per unit area. The formula is pressure = force ÷ area. This means the same force gives a larger pressure on a smaller area, which is why knives are sharp and snowshoes are wide. Force is measured in newtons (N), area in square metres (m²), and the pressure in newtons per square metre (N/m²), also called pascals (Pa). If area is in cm² the unit is N/cm².

bullets: m/s to km/h: multiply by **3.6** (× 3600 seconds per hour ÷ 1000 metres per km). 10 m/s = 36 km/h.
km/h to m/s: divide by 3.6. 90 km/h = 25 m/s.
g/cm³ to kg/m³: multiply by **1000**. 8.5 g/cm³ = 8500 kg/m³. 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.
Area: 1 m² = 100 × 100 = **10 000 cm²**. So N/cm² to N/m²: multiply by 10 000.
Convert time in minutes to hours by dividing by 60; seconds to hours by dividing by 3600.
Show the conversion step in your working to earn the method mark.
core.p: Compound units are converted in stages, converting each part separately. This is where many marks are lost. For speed you convert the distance unit and the time unit; for density the mass and volume units; for pressure the force and area units. The conversion factors for area and volume are the **squares and cubes** of the length conversion, not the same number as the length conversion.

bullets: Pay = rate per hour × hours worked; rate = pay ÷ hours.
Example: £92 for 8 hours gives £92 ÷ 8 = £11.50 per hour.
Unit price = price ÷ quantity (e.g. pence per gram).
Best buy: 500 g for £1.20 costs 120 ÷ 500 = 0.24 p per g, and 750 g for £1.65 costs 165 ÷ 750 = 0.22 p per g, so the larger pack is better value.
Alternative method: find the amount per £1 or per 1p; the larger amount is better value.
Overtime is often paid at 'time and a half' (× 1.5) or double time (× 2).
State a conclusion: 'the 750 g pack is better value because it costs less per gram'.
core.h: Rates of pay and unit pricing
core.p: A **rate of pay** is an amount of money per unit of time, e.g. £12.50 per hour. **Unit pricing** means finding the price per one unit (per gram, per litre, per item) so that different sizes or offers can be compared fairly. This is another kind of compound measure. The best value is the one with the **lowest price per unit** or the **most quantity per pound**.

bullets: Write the formula (e.g. density = mass ÷ volume), then substitute.
Check units agree before calculating (convert first).
Rearrangements: if X = Y ÷ Z then Y = X × Z and Z = Y ÷ X.
All three formulas share this shape, so one skill covers all.
'Per' in a question means divide; 'for each' also signals a rate.
For multi-step problems, find intermediate values first (e.g. volume of a cylinder, then mass).
Round only at the end and include the unit.
core.h: Rearranging and choosing the correct formula
core.p: Every problem in this topic is a single relationship between three quantities, so the main skill is to identify which quantity you are asked for and rearrange accordingly. Writing the formula first, substituting numbers with units, and then evaluating is the most reliable approach. The triangle method is fine for recall, but make sure you can also rearrange algebraically, because the same patterns occur in algebra questions and proof-like 'show that' tasks.

bullets: Constant speed: the distance-time graph is a straight line through the origin; distance ∝ time.
Fixed distance: doubling the speed halves the time.
Fixed mass: a material twice as dense occupies half the volume.
Fixed force: doubling the area halves the pressure.
Density is the gradient of a graph of mass against volume.
Higher tier: in algebra, write s = k / t or P = F / A and recognise inverse proportion.
Use proportion to check answers: if one quantity increases, does the other change in the expected direction?
core.p: Compound measures are examples of proportion. For a constant speed, distance is **directly proportional** to time. For a fixed distance, time is **inversely proportional** to speed. For a fixed mass, volume is inversely proportional to density, and for a fixed force, pressure is inversely proportional to area. Recognising this lets you solve problems without full calculation, and links the topic to graphs and algebra.

bullets: Fuel use, e.g. a car at 45 mph for 2 hours travels 90 miles.
Mass of a wall, metal or water tank: volume first, then mass = density × volume.
Pressure under a table: weight shared between legs, area in m² or cm² - convert if needed.
Two-stage speed problems: find time for each part, add for the total.
A catch: the question may give time in minutes and speed in km/h; convert before substituting.
Estimation: round to one significant figure to check the size of your answer.
Write the conclusion in words if the question asks you to 'compare' or 'decide'.
core.p: Higher tier questions combine these formulae with other skills such as volume, percentages, ratio or unit conversion, and may be set in context with no formula given. You are expected to plan the steps, work with consistent units and communicate clearly. Layout your working so the examiner can award method marks even if the final answer is wrong.

bullets: Gradient of mass-volume graph = density.
Gradient of distance-time graph = speed.
Gradient of force-area graph = pressure.
Always work out the gradient using a large triangle for accuracy.
State the unit of the gradient: unit of vertical axis per unit of horizontal axis.
A steeper line on a mass-volume graph represents a denser material.
Use the graph to read an intermediate value, then check it with the formula.
core.h: Graphs and tables for compound measures
core.p: Data on mass and volume, or force and area, may be given in a table or graph. A graph of mass against volume for one material is a straight line through the origin whose gradient is the density. Reading and interpreting such graphs follows the same logic as distance-time graphs: the gradient of a graph of y against x is y per x, which is a compound unit.

bullets: Three known/unknown quantities: write which two you have and which you want.
Speed questions use distance and time; density questions use mass and volume; pressure questions use force and area.
If the answer unit is km/h, distance must be in km and time in hours.
If the answer unit is g/cm³, mass must be in g and volume in cm³; if kg/m³, use kg and m³.
If the answer unit is N/m² (Pa), force must be in N and area in m².
Mixed units such as 'minutes' and 'km' are a signal that a conversion step is needed.
Write the unit after every line of working so that errors show up early.
core.h: Reading the question: which formula, which units?
core.p: Most compound-measure questions are won or lost before any arithmetic, in how the question is read. The word per means divide, so miles per hour is miles ÷ hours and pence per gram is pence ÷ grams. Underline the two quantities you are given and the one you must find, then pick the formula that links them and write it down. Check the units of the numbers match the units wanted in the answer, and convert first if they do not.

bullets: Gradient = rise ÷ run = (distance 2 − distance 1) ÷ (time 2 − time 1).
Straight sloping line = constant speed; steeper = faster.
Horizontal line = stationary, speed 0.
Line sloping down = moving back towards the start (the speed is still the size of the gradient).
Average speed for the whole journey = total distance travelled ÷ total time, including stops.
Distance from the start is not the same as total distance travelled when the object returns.
Read the scales carefully: one square may not equal one unit.
A curve that gets steeper means the object is speeding up.
core.h: Using a distance-time graph to calculate speed
core.p: On a distance-time graph the vertical axis is distance and the horizontal axis is time, so the gradient of a straight section is change in distance ÷ change in time, which is exactly the speed. A steeper line means a faster speed, a horizontal line means the object is stationary, and a line sloping down means the object is returning towards the start. To find a speed, choose two clear points on the straight section, subtract the distances for the rise and the times for the run, then divide. A curved line means the speed is changing, and the speed at a moment is found from the gradient of a tangent.

bullets: Cuboid: V = l × w × h.
Prism: V = area of cross-section × length.
Cylinder: V = πr²h (r is the radius, half the diameter).
1 cm³ of water has mass 1 g, so water has density 1 g/cm³ (1000 kg/m³).
1 litre = 1000 cm³ and 1 m³ = 1 000 000 cm³.
Mass = density × volume; volume = mass ÷ density.
Check units: mass in g with volume in cm³ gives g/cm³.
If two materials are combined, find total mass ÷ total volume (not the average of the densities).
core.h: Density and the volumes you need
core.p: Density questions often need a volume first. A cuboid has volume length × width × height, a prism has volume cross-sectional area × length, and a cylinder has volume πr²h. Once volume is found in cm³ and mass in g, density is mass ÷ volume in g/cm³, and multiplying by 1000 gives kg/m³. Density can also be used to find a missing mass (mass = density × volume) or a missing volume (volume = mass ÷ density), and objects with a density below that of water float.

bullets: P = F ÷ A; F = P × A; A = F ÷ P.
Units: N/m², which is the same as the pascal (Pa).
Area ÷ 5 means pressure × 5 for a constant force (inverse proportion).
Convert cm² to m² by dividing by 10 000.
Larger force on the same area gives a larger pressure (direct proportion).
Spread the force over a bigger area to reduce pressure (snowshoes, wide tyres).
Concentrate the force on a tiny area to increase pressure (needles, knives).
Show the substitution line (e.g. P = 600 ÷ 0.25) before the answer.
core.p: Pressure tells you how concentrated a force is: the same force acting on a smaller area gives a larger pressure. A force of 600 N on 0.25 m² gives 2400 N/m², but on 0.05 m² it gives 12 000 N/m², five times greater because the area is five times smaller. This is why a sharp knife cuts better than a blunt one and why snowshoes stop you sinking. In calculations, make sure the force is in newtons and the area in m², then divide force by area, and use rearrangements to find force or area when pressure is given.

exam: **1-mark**: substitute or give the correct unit; **2 marks**: correct formula with substituted values and answer; **3-4 marks**: multi-step problems with conversion.
Always **write the formula first**, then substitute: this scores a method mark even with arithmetic slips.
Command words: 'Work out' and 'Calculate' need working and a unit; 'Show that' needs a full chain to a given value; 'Compare' needs a conclusion.
Convert units **before** substituting: minutes to hours, cm² to m², g to kg - and write the conversion factor.
For average speed questions: 'total distance ÷ total time' is the key phrase; show both totals.
Distance-time graph descriptions: say 'stationary', 'returns', 'faster', and quote the speed with units for each stage.
Unit pricing: finish with a sentence naming the better buy and the reason (e.g. 'costs less per gram').
Density problems often need a volume formula first - work out volume, then mass or density.
On non-calculator papers, simplify using cancelling and friendly numbers, and show each step.
Check that the answer is sensible: a person walking at 70 km/h is not realistic.
Give a final answer with the right accuracy, e.g. 3 significant figures if asked.
**Overtime and pay problems:** work out normal pay and overtime pay separately (hours × rate, then overtime hours × overtime rate), then add the two amounts; show each line.

mistakes.r: Convert time to hours (0.5 h) before dividing.
mistakes.w: Using minutes in a speed in km/h, e.g. 150 ÷ 30 for a 30-minute journey.

mistakes.r: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time.
mistakes.w: Finding average speed by averaging the two speeds.

mistakes.r: 1 m² = 100 × 100 = 10 000 cm²; areas are squared, volumes cubed.

mistakes.w: Converting g/cm³ to kg/m³ by multiplying by 100 or not at all.

mistakes.r: Include the compound unit: g/cm³, km/h, N/m².
mistakes.w: Forgetting units or writing the wrong unit, e.g. density in g.

mistakes.r: Density = mass ÷ volume. Write the formula first.
mistakes.w: Dividing the wrong way round (e.g. volume ÷ mass).

mistakes.r: Use 1/3 hour (or 20 ÷ 60) to avoid rounding errors.

mistakes.w: Reading a horizontal line on a distance-time graph as constant speed.

mistakes.r: Compare price per unit (or amount per £1).
mistakes.w: Choosing the pack with the lower price as the best buy without comparing quantity.
Dividing 3000 m by 15 minutes and calling the answer km/h.

summary: Use compound measures: calculate speed, density and pressure using speed = distance ÷ time, density = mass ÷ volume and pressure = force ÷ area, rearrange them, convert units, and solve rate problems such as pay and unit price. It matters because it is a frequent multi-step calculation on both Higher papers.

terms.d: A unit made by combining two other units, such as km/h or g/cm³, describing a rate.
The distance travelled per unit of time: speed = distance ÷ time.
Total distance travelled divided by the total time taken.
A graph showing distance travelled against time, where the gradient represents speed.
The steepness of a line: the change in the vertical value divided by the change in the horizontal value.
Not moving; shown as a horizontal line on a distance-time graph.
Mass per unit volume: density = mass ÷ volume.
The amount of matter in an object, measured in grams or kilograms.
The amount of space occupied by an object, measured in cm³ or m³.
Force per unit area: pressure = force ÷ area.
A push or pull, measured in newtons (N).
The unit of pressure; 1 Pa = 1 N/m².
A measure of how one quantity changes in relation to another, shown by 'per'.
The amount of money paid per unit of time, such as pounds per hour.
The cost of one unit of a quantity, used to compare value for money.
Two quantities where one increases as the other decreases so their product stays constant.
Speed that does not change; shown by a straight sloping line on a distance-time graph.
The number you multiply or divide by to change units, such as 3.6 for m/s to km/h or 1000 for g/cm³ to kg/m³.
The area of the face you get when you cut through a prism; volume of a prism = cross-sectional area × length.
The SI unit of density; 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³.

worked.q: A car travels 150 km in 2 hours 30 minutes, then 90 km in 1 hour 30 minutes. Work out its average speed for the whole journey. (3 marks)
steps: Average speed = total distance ÷ total time = 240 ÷ 4 = 60.

worked.q: A metal block measures 8 cm by 5 cm by 3 cm and has mass 1.02 kg. Work out its density in g/cm³, and give it in kg/m³. (4 marks)

worked.ans: 2400 N/m² and 12 000 N/m²; the smaller area gives 5 times the pressure
worked.q: A force of 600 N acts on an area of 0.25 m². Work out the pressure. The same force acts on an area of 0.05 m². Compare the two pressures. (3 marks)
steps: Area is 5 times smaller so pressure is 5 times bigger (12 000 ÷ 2400 = 5).
